note: Multiply each channel by its `scale` to reach unit variance. Per-CHANNEL, not per-epoch: a per-epoch z-score would normalise away the amplitude difference that defines N3.
reference: single-channel EEG scale from eeg_normalization.json is 15849.46; channel 0 here should land close to it.

this_file.method: every epoch of all 137 training recordings

disagrees_with_eeg_normalization_json.which_is_right: this one. Recomputing over the full training split from the SINGLE-channel tensors reproduces 4.3693e-05 exactly, so the difference is the estimator, not the data - and channel 0 is verified bit-identical to those tensors on all 196 recordings.
disagrees_with_eeg_normalization_json.why_the_old_estimate_is_biased: Sampling a FIXED 120 epochs per recording weights every recording equally, regardless of length. Per-recording amplitude spans 30x in this data (ST7191J0 3.1e-04 V against SC4552F0 1.0e-05 V), and the high-amplitude ST telemetry recordings are SHORTER than the SC cassette ones. Equal-weighting therefore over-represents them and inflates the global std by ~44%.
disagrees_with_eeg_normalization_json.does_it_invalidate_anything: No. EEG_SCALE is an input contract, not a claim about the world: a model trained and evaluated at 15849.46 is self-consistent, and BatchNorm after the first convolution makes the network largely invariant to a constant input scale. The practical effect on student_N2multiscale is that its input variance is ~0.69 rather than 1.0 - which is why its own log reported an input std of 0.457 rather than ~1.
disagrees_with_eeg_normalization_json.consequence_for_the_mc_run: It changes channel 0's scale from 15849.46 to 22886.88, so the multi-channel run varies the channel-0 scale as well as adding channels. A mild confound, recorded rather than hidden. Using the biased value to preserve comparability would mean knowingly shipping a wrong normalisation into a new model.
